parsed.headline: President Mahama commends Ghana's re-election to the UN Human Rights Council

pages.text: President John Dramani Mahama has commended Ghana's Minister of Foreign Affairs, Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs for leading a successful campaign for re-election to the United Nations Human Rights Council (UNHRC). Speaking at the commissioning of new ambassadors at the Jubilee House in Accra on Friday, October 16, 2026, the President stated that the re-election for the 2027–2029 term places a renewed responsibility on the country to contribute with purpose and credibility. He expressed expectation that Ghana's Mission in Geneva will translate this confidence into constructive service on the council. Ghana's current term, which began following an election in 2023, is scheduled to end on December 31, 2026. During elections held by the UN General Assembly in New York on October 13, 2026, Ghana secured 173 votes out of 181 valid ballots. This result placed Ghana joint second globally with Kuwait and Nepal. Within the African group, Zambia received 177 votes, while Nigeria secured 172 votes. Ghana's upcoming term on the 47-member council is scheduled to run from January 1, 2027, to December 31, 2029.

pages.text: President John Dramani Mahama stated that Ghana's application to join the BRICS bloc is a strategy to broaden development partnerships and deepen South-South cooperation. parsed.headline: War in Yemen threatens archaeological sites and fuels antiquities trafficking concerns

pages.text: Renewed offensives by the Houthi militia in Yemen have raised concerns regarding the fate of cultural heritage following more than a decade of conflict, destruction, and looting. While the specific impact of recent fighting on museum collections and archaeological sites has yet to be established, researchers report significant damage to the country's history. Mohammed Ali Thamer, the director general of cultural statistics at the Sanaa-based Ministry of Culture, estimates that approximately 477 of the 2,318 archaeological sites documented by Yemen’s Archaeological Atlas in 2014 have undergone total or partial destruction during the war. Thamer’s research for the Sanaa Center, which utilizes ministry records, statistical data, and the Yemen Data Project, also documents 775 destructive operations affecting cultural sites between the start of the civil war in 2014 and 2025.

The conflict and fragmented authority have created conditions for the theft, smuggling, and sale of antiquities to international buyers. Thamer’s research describes a wave of looting during the current war, specifically targeting ancient tombs and archaeological sites in Marib, Al-Jawf, and Shabwa by individuals searching for gold and saleable artifacts. While comprehensive national statistics on stolen artifacts are unavailable, estimates in Thamer's research place the number of Yemeni artifacts held abroad between 10,000 and 14,000. Additionally, Yemen’s antiquities authorities have listed 8,000 objects they say were smuggled out during the war. Saleh Al-Baydani, president of the Anaween Center for Research and Transformation Studies in Aden, stated that the deterioration of state institutions has allowed trafficking to flourish.

parsed.headline: BNP sells 70 nomination forms for reserved women’s seat by-election in Bangladesh

pages.text: The Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) sold 70 nomination forms to female candidates on Friday for a by-election to reserved women’s seat No. 23 in the 13th Jatiya Sangsad. According to BNP Media Cell member Sairul Kabir Khan and sources at the party’s central office, the forms were distributed at the party's central office in Nayapaltan, Dhaka, between 10 a.m. and 5 p.m. on Friday. Each form cost Tk 5,000, totaling Tk 350,000 in revenue for the party. Candidates who proceed to submit completed forms must pay an additional Tk 50,000, resulting in a total cost of Tk 55,000 per aspirant. Aspiring candidates have been instructed to submit their completed forms to the BNP central office between 10 a.m. and 5 p.m. on Saturday, October 17. The by-election for the vacant seat is scheduled for November 12, according to the Election Commission. The seat became vacant following the resignation of previous occupant Ferdousy Ahmed Mishti on October 1, 2026.

parsed.headline: Student organizations at Jagannath University hold beef feast to protest slaughter ban

pages.text: Leaders of the Jagannath University Central Students’ Union (JnUCSU) and several other student organizations held a feast on the Jagannath University campus in Bangladesh on October 16, 2026. The organizers described the event, which involved the slaughter of a cow, as a protest against a university directive banning animal slaughter on the premises. According to Abdul Alim Arif, general secretary of JnUCSU and president of the JnU unit of the pro-Jamaat-e-Islami student organization Islami Chhatra Shibir, the feast was held in protest against what he called “an unreasonable administrative decision.” Arif claimed that almost all student organizations on campus participated in the event. Organizers stated they viewed the slaughter restriction as an unreasonable curb on cultural practices and student food choices. On the morning of October 16, 2026, students arranged the slaughter of a cow on the road between the mathematics department and the vice-chancellor’s building, later distributing cooked beef and khichuri to students. Organizers said the cost of the cow was met through donations and a registration fee of Tk 70.

The protest follows a dispute that began on the night of October 12, 2026, when students from the 2021-22 academic session of the Islamic history and culture department arranged to cook beef khichuri near the university’s open-air stage to celebrate completing their undergraduate studies. At that time, several Hindu students objected to the location, stating it was too close to the central temple, and it was alleged that bricks from the temple had been used to construct the cooking stove. Regarding the October 16 event, Acting Proctor Prof Md Azam Khan told The Daily Star that the university administration had verbally withdrawn the slaughter restriction and permitted the program on the condition that the slaughter be conducted hygienically under university supervision. Khan stated that university officials and police monitored the event and that no untoward incident occurred.

parsed.headline: Israeli settlers attack Palestinian olive farmers and Washington Post journalist in West Bank

pages.text: Masked Israeli settlers wielding clubs, slingshots, and other weapons attacked Palestinian olive farmers and a Washington Post photographer in the occupied West Bank on Friday, October 15, 2026. The coordinated movement, described as part of yearly attacks to disrupt the annual olive harvest, resulted in injuries to at least 20 people across eight villages, according to Palestinian authorities. Witnesses reported that settlers also burned cars and approximately a dozen olive trees during the violence. In the town of Abu Falah, near Ramallah, at least 80 settlers—some carrying firearms or clubs—gathered to stop harvesting. When some Palestinians used rocks to defend themselves, the Israeli military reportedly fired teargas in their direction. The Israeli Foreign Press Association stated that such violent attacks against journalists and civilians have been a recurring issue and that calls for action have been ignored by Israeli authorities. The United Nations noted that levels of settler violence have reached an all-time high this year, with the past two weeks seeing more attacks than the entire previous harvest season.

Among those injured was Heidi Levine, a veteran photographer for The Washington Post, who was beaten during an attack that witnesses said lasted more than 10 minutes. Levine, who was wearing a protective vest clearly marked as “press,” reported being pushed to the ground and kicked. Settlers also reportedly stole her passport, phone, wallet, and camera equipment. Levine was treated at a hospital in Ramallah for injuries to her leg and hand. Washington Post Executive Editor Matt Murray denounced the attack as unwarranted and called for a thorough investigation. Reporters Without Borders characterized the incident as “brazen violence.” Local officials reported that among the Palestinian injuries were four dual Palestinian-American citizens, including Majdi Fheed, who sustained head and neck wounds. In response to the reports of violence, a spokesperson for the US State Department said they were aware of the situation.

The violence occurred amid broader diplomatic tensions regarding West Bank settlements. On October 15, 2026, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi met with Israeli President Isaac Herzog in Azerbaijan. During the meeting, Wang told Herzog that the “Palestinian question” is the “greatest historical injustice of this century” and urged Israel to stop the “forced establishment” of settlements in the West Bank. Herzog stated the meeting focused on Middle East relations and emphasized Israel's desire for peace alongside strategic security threats from Iran and its proxies.
